structure.title: I
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway reflecting on his father’s advice to reserve judgment due to unequal advantages, a habit that has made him a confidant but left him disillusioned after returning from the East, where he witnessed moral chaos in privileged society—except for Jay Gatsby, whose extraordinary hope and romantic readiness he singles out as exceptional. In the spring of 1922, Nick rents a modest bungalow in West Egg for eighty dollars a month, acquiring an old Dodge, a dog (which soon runs away), and a Finnish housekeeper, while filling his shelves with twelve volumes on banking to cultivate intellectual and financial renewal. After feeling isolated, he gains a sense of belonging when a stranger asks him for directions to West Egg village; later, he drives by car to East Egg to dine with his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, whom he knew at Yale, meeting the enigmatic Jordan Baker, who lies motionless on a couch. During dinner, Tom aggressively espouses racist pseudoscience from The Rise of the Coloured Empires, a telephone call reveals his affair in New York (confirmed by Jordan), and Daisy, shaken, expresses bitter cynicism by saying she hopes her daughter will be a 'beautiful little fool.' After Jordan reads aloud from the Saturday Evening Post and departs, Daisy teases Nick about marrying Jordan, while Tom coldly disapproves of her independence; Nick denies rumors he is engaged to a woman out West, explaining the gossip prompted his move East. As he drives home to West Egg, he pauses in his yard and sees Gatsby standing on the lawn, arms outstretched toward a distant green light across the bay, trembling before vanishing into the night.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer Sunday afternoon, Nick Carraway travels by train with Tom Buchanan from West Egg to the valley of ashes, where Tom introduces him to Myrtle Wilson, who lives above her husband George Wilson’s run-down garage beneath the looming eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg; Tom and Myrtle arrange to meet in New York, with Myrtle riding separately on the train to avoid social scrutiny, and upon arrival, she purchases a dog, cold cream, perfume, and magazines before taking a lavender taxicab to her apartment on 158th Street, where she changes into a cream chiffon dress and hosts a chaotic gathering with her sister Catherine and the McKees, during which alcohol flows freely, Myrtle openly flirts with Tom, and Catherine falsely claims Daisy is Catholic and preventing their divorce, leading Myrtle to drunkenly shout Daisy’s name until Tom breaks her nose with a single blow, triggering screams, frantic attempts to clean the blood with a copy of Town Tattle, and the collapse of the party as Mr. McKee stumbles out and later invites Nick to lunch in the elevator, leaving Nick alone in the cold, dim interior of Pennsylvania Station at dawn waiting for a train.

structure.title: III
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway arriving at Jay Gatsby’s mansion on Long Island late Saturday evening by car, joining a throng of uninvited guests who have come from New York in Rolls-Royces and station wagons, drawn by the opulent party featuring an orchestra, endless cocktails, and lavish buffets. Amid rumors that Gatsby killed a man or was a German spy, Nick Carraway wanders among the crowd without meeting the host until he unexpectedly encounters Gatsby himself—revealed as a young, refined man with a rare smile—who invites him to fly in his new hydroplane at nine the next morning. Jordan Baker is called away by Gatsby’s butler and returns visibly shaken, refusing to disclose the nature of their conversation, while drunken chaos erupts as Owl Eyes crashes Gatsby’s coupé into a wall, claiming he wasn’t driving; as Nick Carraway departs at two a.m., he sees Gatsby standing alone on the porch, formally bidding farewell. The chapter concludes with Nick Carraway reflecting on his ordinary life in New York, commuting on foot to the Probity Trust, dining at the Yale Club, walking past the Murray Hill Hotel to Pennsylvania Station, and rekindling a quiet fascination with Jordan Baker, whom he later discovers cheated in a golf tournament and lied about damaging a borrowed car, yet he clings to his self-perceived honesty as his defining virtue.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning, Gatsby’s mansion erupts in chaotic revelry as guests from East Egg, West Egg, and New York arrive by car, filling the lawn with eccentric figures like the Chester Beckers, Hammerheads, and Klipspringer, while spreading wild rumors about Gatsby’s identity—claiming he killed a man or is related to Von Hindenburg—none knowing his true past. Later that day, Gatsby arrives at Nick Carraway’s door in his cream-colored car with a three-noted horn, inviting him to lunch; during the drive, Gatsby reveals an elaborate, contradictory personal history—including Oxford education, European aristocratic life, and wartime heroism with medals from Montenegro—backed by physical proof like a photograph from Trinity Quad and the Orderi di Danilo, leaving Nick Carraway shaken by its improbable veracity. At noon in a cellar restaurant on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick Carraway to Meyer Wolfshiem, a grotesque figure with hair growing from his nostrils and cuff buttons made of human molars, who recounts the murder of Rosy Rosenthal and later reveals he fixed the 1919 World Series, shocking Nick Carraway; moments later, Nick Carraway spots Tom Buchanan across the room but Gatsby vanishes before an introduction can occur. In a reflective interlude, Jordan Baker recounts her memories of Daisy Fay in 1917 Louisville, where she first met Lieutenant Gatsby in his white roadster, and describes Daisy’s subsequent engagement to Tom Buchanan, her drunken wedding day ordeal with the $350,000 pearl necklace, and their later life in Chicago after Tom’s car crash with a chambermaid. Finally, at twilight, Jordan and Nick Carraway ride in a victoria through Central Park, where Jordan reveals Gatsby bought his mansion solely so Daisy could see the green light across the bay, and he now asks Nick Carraway to invite Daisy to tea so he can reunite with her unseen, a modest request after years of elaborate preparation that shifts Nick Carraway’s focus from Gatsby’s dream to Jordan herself.

structure.title: V
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick returning to his modest West Egg home at night to find Gatsby’s mansion brilliantly lit but silent, prompting Gatsby to awkwardly invite him to Coney Island or a swim—both declined—before reluctantly asking Nick to arrange a tea meeting with Daisy. The next day, heavy rain falls as Gatsby sends a gardener to cut Nick’s lawn and delivers a greenhouse of flowers; when Daisy arrives by large open car with her chauffeur Ferdie, Gatsby emerges pale and trembling, nearly knocking over a mantelpiece clock in their stiff, emotional reunion that ends with Daisy’s tears and Gatsby’s sudden radiant joy. After the rain stops, Gatsby fervently invites Daisy to tour his mansion on foot via the big postern gate, showcasing opulent rooms including Marie Antoinette music-rooms and Restoration Salons, culminating in a display of imported silk and linen shirts that overwhelms Daisy into uncontrollable sobs as Gatsby stares at her in awe. Later, Gatsby reveals the green light on Daisy’s dock has lost its symbolic power, shows Nick and Daisy photographs of Dan Cody and his youthful self in yachting gear, and shares newspaper clippings about her; he abruptly ends a phone call about a 'small town' misunderstanding, and when the rain clears slightly, Daisy whimsically wishes to put Gatsby inside pink and golden clouds. Gatsby summons Klipspringer, who reluctantly plays piano as they sit in shadowed silence, until Nick departs, observing Gatsby’s sudden doubt about his happiness as he clutches Daisy’s hand, utterly captivated by her voice.

structure.title: VI
characters_present: the woman in the brown riding-habit
structure.summary: The chapter opens with a New York reporter arriving at Gatsby’s mansion seeking a statement, revealing the growing mythos surrounding him through rumors like his alleged residence in a movable house-boat along Long Island; the narrative then turns to Gatsby’s origins as James Gatz of North Dakota, who changed his name after encountering Dan Cody’s yacht on Lake Superior, spent five years aboard Cody’s vessel serving in roles from steward to jailor, and absorbed the persona of Jay Gatsby during travels across continents, only to be left with no inheritance after Cody’s death—manipulated by Ella Kaye—but with a fully formed identity. Later, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon when Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit arrive unexpectedly on horseback; Gatsby, visibly nervous, insists they stay for drinks and supper, but their cold indifference is underscored when Sloane quietly prevents Gatsby from joining their dinner invitation, leaving him standing in hat and coat as they ride away. Days later, Tom and Daisy attend one of Gatsby’s extravagant parties at twilight, where Daisy is uncomfortable with West Egg’s vulgarity yet emotionally stirred by Gatsby’s charm; amid drunken chaos involving guests like Miss Baedeker and Doctor Civet, Gatsby dances with Daisy, attempts to kiss her cheek, and later confides in Nick Carraway his desperate belief that he can repeat the past by having Daisy declare she never loved Tom so they can return to Louisville and restart their relationship as it was five years earlier, recalling a moonlit autumn night when he first kissed her and believed his idealized vision had become real.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On the hottest day of summer, Nick arrives by train at the Buchanans’ house to find Gatsby waiting, having dismissed his servants and replaced them with relatives of Meyer Wolfsheim; during lunch, Daisy openly kisses Gatsby, shocking Tom, who confronts Gatsby’s background and mocks his claim of attending Oxford, leading Tom to insist they drive to town in separate cars — Gatsby in his yellow car with Daisy, Tom with Nick and Jordan in the coupé. After stopping at Wilson’s garage in the Valley of Ashes under the faded eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, where Wilson reveals he has become suspicious of Myrtle’s infidelity and plans to take her away, the group proceeds to the Plaza Hotel in New York, where Tom exposes Gatsby’s bootlegging ties to Wolfsheim; Daisy, overwhelmed, admits she once loved both Tom and Gatsby but refuses to renounce Tom entirely, prompting Tom to order them to leave together. Later, Myrtle Wilson runs from her garage into the dusk and is struck and killed by a speeding yellow car — Michaelis, who witnesses the aftermath, tells police it was light green, though uncertain; Tom and Nick arrive at the scene to find Wilson in anguish, and Tom denies owning the car, claiming his own is blue and he was in New York. That night, Nick refuses to enter the Buchanans’ house and waits outside, where Gatsby emerges to confess Daisy was driving the car that killed Myrtle and intends to take the blame; Nick discovers Tom and Daisy calmly eating together in the kitchen, already reconciled, before returning to find Gatsby standing vigil in the moonlight, guarding a dream that no longer exists.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: On the dawn after a sleepless night haunted by a foghorn, Nick Carraway rushes to Gatsby’s mansion upon hearing a taxi arrive, finding Gatsby dejected after waiting all night for Daisy to appear at her window—she briefly looked out before turning off the light. Inside the vast, dusty, and neglected house, they stumble through opulent rooms searching for cigarettes, eventually smoking on the French windows as Nick Carraway urges Gatsby to flee to Atlantic City or Montreal; Gatsby refuses, clinging to the hope that Daisy will choose him, and in a vulnerable recounting, reveals how he falsely led her to believe he was wealthy during their youthful romance, becoming irrevocably bound to an idealized version of her. Later, at dawn, as golden light fills the house, Gatsby insists Daisy never truly loved Tom and recounts his miserable train journey to Louisville after returning from war, revisiting places tied to her memory, feeling he left her behind. He reveals he has never used his pool all summer, and after breakfast, Nick Carraway misses two trains, unable to leave, shouting that Gatsby is worth more than 'the whole damn bunch put together,' to which Gatsby responds with a radiant smile. Meanwhile, in West Egg, George Wilson, consumed by grief and convinced Myrtle was killed by the driver of a yellow car, travels on foot from his garage to Port Roosevelt and then Gad’s Hill, buying an uneaten sandwich and coffee, before arriving in West Egg by 2:30 p.m., having learned Gatsby’s name and asking for directions to his house. At two o’clock, Gatsby dons his bathing suit, instructs the butler to bring any calls to him at the pool, declines help as he carries a pneumatic mattress alone to the water, and waits—no call comes. The butler waits until four, believing no one will call; moments later, gunshots are heard, and Nick Carraway arrives to find Gatsby’s body floating in the pool, the mattress drifting with faint ripples, while the gardener discovers Wilson’s body in the grass, completing the tragedy.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: Following Gatsby’s death, Nick Carraway is left alone to manage the chaotic influx of police, photographers, and reporters at Gatsby’s mansion, while curious children sneak through the yard to stare at the pool; despite his desperate attempts to contact Daisy and Meyer Wolfsheim via phone, letter, and butler-delivered messages, both remain silent, and a Chicago call mistakenly assumes Gatsby is alive before abruptly disconnecting upon learning of his death. On the third day, Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives by train from Minnesota, visibly shaken by his son’s opulent estate and clutching a childhood book containing Gatsby’s self-improvement schedule, yet only he and a Lutheran minister attend the funeral, as Klipspringer refuses to come for a picnic and Wolfsheim cites personal principles to avoid involvement; in a thick drizzle at five o’clock, a procession of three cars—motor hearse, limousine, and station wagon—arrives at the cemetery, where Nick Carraway recognizes the man with owl-eyed glasses, who had once marveled at Gatsby’s books, now splashing through the rain to pay his respects, murmuring 'Amen to that' when someone quotes 'Blessed are the dead that the rain falls on' and later calls Gatsby 'the poor son-of-a-bitch.' Afterward, Nick Carraway reflects on his nostalgic train journeys to the Midwest during Christmas, contrasting their warmth with his haunting memory of West Egg as a grotesque El Greco painting, leading him to decide to return home; he meets Jordan Baker, who reveals she is engaged to another man, and though they discuss their broken relationship and her accusation of his dishonesty, he admits he is too old to lie to himself. Finally, after selling his car and packing his trunk, Nick Carraway walks alone to Gatsby’s empty house, erases an obscene word scrawled on the steps, and wanders to the beach, meditating on how Gatsby’s dream of the green light was already behind him, ending with the metaphor that humanity, like boats, is borne back ceaselessly into the past.

plot_summary.plot_summary:
In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway moves to West Egg, Long Island, seeking renewal after the war, renting a modest home next to the extravagant mansion of the enigmatic Jay Gatsby. Through his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom—a wealthy, arrogant Yale alumnus with a mistress, Myrtle Wilson—Nick is drawn into the opulent yet morally hollow world of East Egg’s elite. He also becomes acquainted with the cynical, detached Jordan Baker, and gradually forms a quiet fascination with Gatsby, whose lavish parties attract hundreds of anonymous guests yet conceal his solitary yearning. Nick learns from Jordan that Gatsby’s entire fortune and mansion were acquired with one purpose: to rekindle a lost romance with Daisy, whom he had met and loved five years earlier as a young officer before being sent overseas.

As Nick becomes Gatsby’s confidant, he facilitates a reunion between Gatsby and Daisy, reigniting their connection amid Gatsby’s grand displays of wealth. But beneath the surface, Gatsby’s idealized vision of Daisy is fragile, built on illusions of class and status he fabricated to win her. Tom, suspicious of Gatsby’s background, confronts him during a tense trip to New York, exposing his bootlegging ties through Meyer Wolfsheim and dismantling his claims of Oxford pedigree. Daisy, overwhelmed, admits she once loved both men but refuses to renounce Tom. That same afternoon, Myrtle Wilson is killed by a speeding yellow car—driven by Daisy, though Gatsby takes the blame. In the aftermath, Tom manipulates George Wilson, Myrtle’s husband, into believing Gatsby was both Myrtle’s lover and her killer. Meanwhile, Gatsby waits in vain for Daisy to call, clinging to the hope she will choose him, even as she retreats with Tom into their insulated world of privilege and indifference.

After Gatsby is shot and killed by George Wilson at his pool, Nick struggles to arrange a funeral, only to find that Gatsby’s so-called friends—those who feasted at his parties—vanish without a trace. Only Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives from Minnesota, proud of his son’s achievements but unaware of the corruption behind them. Nick, disillusioned by the moral decay he has witnessed, rejects the East and resolves to return home. He breaks with Jordan Baker, who is now engaged to another man, and reflects on Gatsby’s tragic dream: the green light across the bay symbolized not just Daisy, but an impossible ideal of renewal and perfection that was already behind him. In the final moments, Nick stands alone on the beach, contemplating how humanity, like boats against the current, is forever borne back ceaselessly into the past.
